extract:primary-0001-aa4049b632.summary: The author frames America’s cause as one of universal human concern, condemns the King–Parliament combination as oppressive usurpation, and notes that the doctrine of Independance has received no published refutation.
plotBeats: The author argues that entrenched custom can initially make wrongdoing appear right, but that time changes opinion.
The King of England’s support for Parliament’s asserted rights is presented as part of a combination that grievously oppresses the people of the country and may be rejected as usurpation.
America’s cause is enlarged into a cause affecting all mankind, particularly where natural rights are attacked.
A delayed new edition is issued after no answer has appeared to refute the Doctrine of Independance.
themes: Custom and the delayed recognition of wrongdoing
Resistance to oppressive and usurped authority
America’s cause as a universal human concern
Independance and the absence of a published refutation

extract:primary-0002-e36801330a.summary: The segment distinguishes society from government, argues that government arises from moral failure to secure freedom and security, sketches representative government as a colony grows, and rebuts the English constitution as a complex union in which hereditary monarchy and aristocracy leave the crown dominant.
plotBeats: Society and government are separated by origin and function: society arises from wants and promotes happiness, while government arises from wickedness and restrains vice.
Government is presented as a necessary evil whose legitimate end is security, and later as a system aimed at freedom and security.
A hypothetical colony moves from direct assembly to frequently elected representatives as growth makes universal meetings impractical.
The English constitution is criticized as complex, imperfect, and built from monarchical and aristocratical tyranny combined with republican materials.
The crown is identified as the constitution's dominant power, while national pride and prejudice obscure constitutional defects.
themes: Society and government have distinct origins and purposes.
Security and freedom are the ends by which government should be judged.
Representation and frequent elections align elected officials with the public.
Simplicity is preferable to constitutional complexity.
Hereditary power and national prejudice undermine political freedom.

passages.title: Society and government distinguished
passages.text:
Society is produced by our wants, and government by our wickedness; 
the former promotes our happiness positively by uniting 
our affections, the latter negatively by restraining our 
vices. The one encourages intercourse, the other creates 
distinctions. The first a patron, the last a punisher.
passages.context: The opening distinction between the two central terms.
passages.significance: It establishes the conceptual opposition that grounds the section's account of political legitimacy.

passages.title: Government's origin and end
passages.text:
Here then is the origin and rise of government; namely, a mode rendered
necessary by the inability of moral virtue to govern the world; here
too is the design and end of government, viz. freedom and security.
passages.context: The conclusion of the hypothetical account of settlers forming government.
passages.significance: It supplies the section's compact statement of why government exists and what it should deliver.

passages.title: Frequent elections preserve common interest
passages.text:
that the elected might never form to themselves an interest 
separate from the electors, prudence will point out the 
propriety of having elections often; because as the elected 
might by that means return and mix again with the general body of the 
electors in a few months, their fidelity to the public will be 
secured by the prudent reflexion of not making a rod for themselves. 
And as this frequent interchange will establish a common interest with 
every part of the community, they will mutually and naturally support 
each other, and on this (not on the unmeaning name of king) depends 
the strength of government, and the happiness of the governed.
passages.context: The proposed development from direct assembly to representative government in a growing colony.
passages.significance: It offers frequent election and shared interest as the practical source of governmental strength and public happiness.

passages.title: English constitution condemned as a mixed tyranny
passages.text:
if we will suffer ourselves to examine the component parts of the
English constitution, we shall find them to be the base remains of two
ancient tyrannies, compounded with some new republican materials.
passages.context: The transition from general principles of governmental simplicity to the English case.
passages.significance: It frames the subsequent analysis of king, peers, and commons as a critique of the constitution's origins.

passages.title: The crown holds the key
passages.text:
That the crown is this overbearing part in the English constitution
needs not be mentioned, and that it derives its whole consequence
merely from being the giver of places and pensions is self-evident,
wherefore, though we have been wise enough to shut and lock a door
against absolute monarchy, we at the same time have been foolish 
enough to put the crown in possession of the key.
passages.context: The critique of the claim that the constitution's three powers effectively check one another.
passages.significance: It names the crown as the decisive power and uses the key image to deny that constitutional checks have excluded monarchy.

passages.title: Prejudice disables constitutional judgment
passages.text:
An inquiry into the constitutional errors in the English form 
of government is at this time highly necessary, for as we are never in a
proper condition of doing justice to others, while we continue under
the influence of some leading partiality, so neither are we capable of
doing it to ourselves while we remain fettered by any obstinate
prejudice.
passages.context: The section's closing call to examine the English form of government without partiality.
passages.significance: It turns the constitutional critique into a demand for freedom from prejudice as a condition of political judgment.

extract:primary-0003-7ed9938aef.summary: This section argues that monarchy and hereditary succession violate natural equality and scriptural authority. It uses the Israelites' requests for kings and English history to portray both arrangements as sources of corruption, unfit rulers, and civil conflict, and contrasts them with republican principles.
plotBeats: The argument begins from original human equality and rejects the division of people into kings and subjects as lacking a natural or religious justification.
The history of the children of Israel is presented as a scriptural warning: Gideon refuses an offered hereditary kingship, and Samuel describes the exactions of a king requested by the people.
Hereditary succession is attacked as an unjust transfer of posterity's rights that can elevate unworthy heirs and become established through fear, superstition, and convenience.
English history, especially conflicts between York and Lancaster, is offered to rebut the claim that hereditary succession prevents civil war.
The section closes by treating the English constitution as weakened by monarchical influence over its republican House of Commons.
themes: the republican part in the constitution of England

entities.name: Monarchy
entities.summary: A form of government that the section rejects as contrary to natural equality and scripture and associates with war, idolatrous homage, corruption, and oppression.
entities.excerpt:
Monarchy is ranked in scripture as one of the sins of the Jews, for
which a curse in reserve is denounced against them.

attributes.authorial-assessment: Rejected as a sinful and oppressive form of government.

there is another and greater distinction for which no truly

subjects.

claims.text: The section attributes wars and confusion in early history to the pride of kings.
claims.excerpt:

claims.text: The author characterizes monarchy as a system opposed by the word of God and attended by bloodshed.
claims.excerpt:
’Tis a form of government
which the word of God bears testimony against, and blood will attend it.

entities.name: Hereditary succession
entities.summary: The inheritance of rule by a king's descendants, which the section calls an unjust imposition on posterity and a source of unfit rulers, regencies, and civil conflict.
entities.excerpt:
To the evil of monarchy we have added that of hereditary succession;
and as the first is a degradation and lessening of ourselves, so the
second, claimed as a matter of right, is an insult and an imposition on
posterity.

attributes.stated-purpose: Defenders claim that it preserves a nation from civil wars.
attributes.authorial-assessment: Rejected as oppressive and as an unjust deprivation of posterity's rights.

as it opens a

extract:primary-0004-799e727fd2.summary: The speaker argues that armed conflict has made reconciliation with Great-Britain untenable and that American independence is necessary for security, peace, and self-government. The section rejects British authority as distant and self-interested, contrasts republican equality with monarchy, and proposes a Continental Congress, Conference, and Charter to establish a continental government.
plotBeats: The speaker treats the struggle between England and America as having passed from debate to armed contest.
Reconciliation is rejected as a dangerous, temporary arrangement that would leave America subject to British interests and future conflict.
Independence is advanced as the condition for continental peace, security, and the ability to make American laws.
A constitutional framework is proposed: annual assemblies, a representative Continental Congress, a Continental Conference, and a Continental Charter.
The section closes by casting America as an asylum for freedom against Old World oppression.
themes: America as an asylum for freedom

extract:primary-0005-0cc95308b4.summary: The pamphlet argues that America is already at the uniquely favorable moment to declare independance: its unity, population, resources, undeveloped land, and productive capacity make collective self-government and naval defense practical now. It rejects renewed British rule as unsafe and politically disabling, recommends a commercially useful fleet, a Continental Charter, religious protection, and large, equal representation, and closes by arguing that a public declaration is necessary for foreign recognition, mediation, and assistance.
plotBeats: The narrator treats separation between England and America as inevitable and argues that the present moment has already made America fit for independance.
America's unity, armed population, lack of debt, and material resources are presented as sufficient foundations for collective action.
A fleet is proposed as both a commercial investment and the necessary means of protecting American property and coasts.
Reliance on Britain for defense is rejected because a former would-be conqueror could turn friendship into slavery and distant ships cannot answer emergencies.
The narrator warns that resubmission to British government would bring ruin, recurring disorder, and foreign obedience, while only Continental authority can regulate Continental affairs.
America's youth and current union are framed as a fleeting opportunity to form a government before population, commerce, and conflicting interests divide the colonies.
The proposed government should begin with a charter or articles that define rights before officials are delegated to execute them.
The section calls for government to protect all conscientious religious professors and for a Continental Charter and large, equal representation to secure rights and restrain concentrated power.
The conclusion contends that declaring independance is necessary to end the contradiction of resistance and British subjection, obtain foreign mediation and aid, and be received by other nations.
themes: Independance as a present and irreversible political necessity
Foreign recognition and the costs of British subjection

passages.title: Strength in unity
passages.text:
It is not in numbers, but in unity, that our great strength lies; yet
our present numbers are sufficient to repel the force of all the world.
passages.context: The narrator opens the practical case for immediate independance by identifying unity rather than population size as America's decisive strength.
passages.significance: This compact formulation states the segment's central measure of collective American capacity.

passages.title: Commerce and protection united
passages.text:
A navy when finished is worth more than it
cost. And is that nice point in national policy, in which commerce and
protection are united.

passages.significance: It captures the economic rationale for naval protection that anchors the section's long maritime argument.

passages.title: Britain cannot defend America

others, the most improper to defend us.

passages.significance: It states the constitutional ordering principle behind the proposed charter: rights and governmental articles precede officeholders.

passages.title: Government's religious duty

all government, to protect all conscientious professors thereof, and I
know of no other business which government hath to do therewith.
passages.context: The narrator defines a limited governmental responsibility amid diverse religious denominations.
passages.significance: The statement gives the segment's clearest rule for the relation between government and religious conscience.

passages.title: The Continental Charter defined
passages.text:
a charter is to be understood as a bond of solemn
obligation, which the whole enters into, to support the right of every
separate part, whether of religion, personal freedom, or property.
passages.context: The narrator returns to a previously introduced Continental Charter and defines its purpose.
passages.significance: This is the segment's operative definition of the constitutional bond proposed for the united colonies.

passages.title: The danger of unequal representation
passages.text:
A small number of electors, or a small number
of representatives, are equally dangerous. But if the number of the
representatives be not only small, but unequal, the danger is
increased.
passages.context: The narrator introduces the Pennsylvania assembly example to argue for a large and equal representative structure.
passages.significance: It concisely supplies the warning against concentrated representative and electoral power.

passages.title: Declaration as settlement
passages.text:
nothing can settle our affairs so expeditiously as an open and 
determined declaration for independance.
passages.context: The concluding case for a declaration introduces reasons involving mediation, foreign assistance, diplomatic status, and trade.
passages.significance: This is the section's direct final proposition linking independance to a workable settlement.

extract:primary-0006-05584f2a63.summary: The appendix renews the case for American independence after condemning the King's Speech and rejecting reconciliation as impracticable and unsafe. It presents independence as the means to unite America, establish an independent constitution through Congress, end the conflict with Britain, and secure lasting peace. It also rebukes Quaker representatives for entering politics without representative authority and for condemning defensive arms while failing to address British violence.
plotBeats: The speaker condemns the King's Speech as openly brutal and tyrannical, treating it as proof that independence is necessary.
America's interest is defined as separation from Britain, whose foreign dependence constrains commerce and legislative power.
Reconciliation is rejected as a complicated and unreliable course because Britain and Parliament cannot be held to future engagements.
The speaker describes America as lacking settled law and government, then urges a prompt, lawful achievement of independence through Congress rather than military power or a mob.
Independence is advanced as the bond that can unite America, create a basis for peace and trade, and allow the formation of an independent constitution.
The address to Quaker representatives argues that their political testimony lacks representative authority and inconsistently censures American defensive force without confronting British aggression.

passages.title: America's interest in separation
passages.speaker: The speaker
passages.text: First. That it is the interest of America to be separated from Britain.
passages.context: The speaker introduces the first of the appendix's two announced heads.
passages.significance: States the central conclusion that organizes the subsequent case against dependence and reconciliation.

passages.title: America without settled government
passages.speaker: The speaker
passages.text:
Without law, without government, without any
other mode of power than what is founded on, and granted by courtesy.
passages.context: The speaker describes the precarious current state of America while comparing independence and reconciliation.
passages.significance: Identifies the absence of a settled legal order as an urgent reason to establish independence on a secure basis.

passages.title: Lawful route to independence
passages.speaker: The speaker
passages.text:
By the legal voice of the people in Congress; 
by a military power; or by a mob:
passages.context: The speaker lists three possible ways America might eventually attain independence.
passages.significance: Frames congressional action as the desirable lawful alternative to military seizure or mob rule.

passages.title: Independence as the bond of union
passages.speaker: The speaker
passages.text:
In short, Independance is the only Bond that 
can tye and keep us together.
passages.context: After urging prompt action, the speaker explains how separation will enable America to negotiate and trade on proper terms.
passages.significance: Condenses independence's proposed political function: to unite America and end the conditions that prolong war.

passages.title: Peace through an independent constitution
passages.speaker: The speaker
passages.text:
Our
plan is peace for ever.
passages.context: Addressing Quaker representatives, the speaker explains that separation and an independent constitution are intended to end the conflict with Britain.
passages.significance: States the claimed end of separation: enduring peace rather than continued contention.

passages.title: Defence rather than conquest
passages.speaker: The speaker
passages.text:
We fight neither for revenge nor conquest; neither from pride nor
passion; we are not insulting the world with our fleets and armies, nor
ravaging the globe for plunder.
passages.context: The speaker rebuts the Quaker testimony's condemnation of American armed action.
passages.significance: Defines the speaker's moral distinction between defensive force and aggressive war.

openQuestions: Will independence be effected by the legal voice of the people in Congress rather than by military power or a mob?
What independent constitution will America form if it achieves separation through Congress?
Will Britain accept peace and reopened trade after America independently redresses its grievances?
